paper.title: How Different Parental Leave Schemes Create Different Take-Up Patterns: Denmark in Nordic Comparison
paper.code_data_availability: No replication code or data-availability statement, and no Statistics Denmark project reference. …

registers.role: outcomes (gender-role attitudes); treatment variables (education, sex, country); sample frame
variables_mentioned: When a mother works for pay, the children suffer
A pre-school child is likely to suffer if his or her mother works
A job is alright but what most women really want is a home and children
A man's job is to earn money; a woman's job is to look after the home and family

registers.name_in_paper: Statistics Denmark (n.d.-b) BARSEL05: Cohabiting parents' leave in the child's first year of life calculated in whole days
registers.role: outcomes (average parental leave days of mothers and fathers)

registers.name_in_paper: Statistics Denmark (n.d.-c) BARSEL04: Parents' leave in the child's first year of life calculated in full days
registers.role: outcomes (fathers' parental leave days by own and partner's education)

registers.name_in_paper: Statistics Denmark (n.d.-a) LBESK03: Employees (seasonally adjusted) by industry
registers.role: background (size of the industrial sector covered by collective-agreement father's quotas)

registers.name_in_paper: NOSOSCO (n.d.) SOCI04: Recipients of daily cash benefits at pregnancy, childbirth and adoption (Nordic Council of Ministers)
registers.role: outcomes (fathers' share of total parental leave days in the Nordic countries)

linkages: the Danish statbank tabulations (BARSEL04/BARSEL05) link cohabiting mothers and fathers of the same child through the parents' 'educational combination', which is how Figure 7 shows father's leave days by both father's and mother's education
survey respondents are not linked to registers: attitudes (EVS) and leave take-up (Statistics Denmark, NOSOSCO) are compared at country and education-group level, not at the individual level

sample.universe: European Values Study respondents of all age groups in the five Nordic countries (Denmark, Finland, Iceland, Norway, Sweden), together with aggregate Danish and Nordic parental leave statistics
sample.unit_of_observation: survey respondent (EVS); country-year (NOSOSCO leave shares); education group of cohabiting parents (Danish leave tabulations)
selection_rules: EVS respondents in the five Nordic countries, mainly the 2017 round, supplemented with the 1990, 1999 and 2008 rounds for one comparative analysis
the whole sample is used (all age groups), not only fathers and mothers
the three gender-role items are recoded into binary agree/disagree variables
education is grouped into lower, medium and higher education as a proxy for social class background
Danish leave averages cover cohabiting parents entitled to leave benefit (Figure 6)
Figure 7 covers cohabiting couples only, and only those where both the mother and the father have taken parental leave
Danish leave-day data only from 2015 onwards, because of a change in registration methods
sample.n_observations: 9,384 EVS respondents in the five Nordic countries in 2017; n = 23,112 pooled over the four rounds plotted in Figure 1; per-item country cell sizes 1,086-3,331 (Table 2 and Figures 2-4)

construction_notes: three EVS items on gender roles are recoded into binary variables by collapsing "strongly agree" with "agree" and "strongly disagree" with "disagree" (p. 4)
education is used as a proxy for social class background (p. 4)
the association between education and agreement is summarised by a gamma coefficient with significance stars (*p < 0.05, **p < 0.01, ***p < 0.001); the statistic and the test are not further named

in 2017 the item "A pre-school child is likely to suffer if his or her mother works" was replaced by "When a mother works for pay, the children suffer" in Finland, Norway and Sweden, but not in Denmark (p. 4)
national sample sizes are reported in the Supplementary File, not in the article
Danish average leave days are reported for cohabiting parents entitled to benefit; only data from 2015 onwards is comparable because of a change in registration methods (p. 8)
Figure 7 reports leave days for cohabiting couples where both parents took leave, by father's and by mother's education
Table 1 compiles paid leave weeks and benefit levels from Duvander et al. (2019), Moss and Duvander (2019) and the OECD family database

implies_edges.to: agreement that "when a mother works for pay, the children suffer"

key_assumptions.assumption: Attitudes measured on the whole sample (all age groups, not only fathers and mothers) capture the social norms relevant to parents' leave behaviour
key_assumptions.supported_by: the authors' statement that social norms are beliefs outside the individual acting as a normative filter (Ajzen, 1988, 1991)

key_assumptions.assumption: The four-point agreement items, collapsed into binary agree/disagree, measure traditional gender-role attitudes (gender ideology)
key_assumptions.supported_by: the recoding is described in the methodology section; no validation reported

key_assumptions.assumption: The 2017 rewording of the item in Finland, Norway and Sweden (but not Denmark) does not undermine comparability across countries and rounds
key_assumptions.supported_by: the authors argue the trend remains similar across the Nordic countries, so the change has a limited impact on the Danish result (p. 4)

threats_discussed: the EVS items are rather extreme statements for a Nordic context, which the authors say could explain the relatively low level of agreement (p. 10)
the EVS survey addresses only the mother's role and includes no question on the paternal role in childcare (p. 7)
one item varies between countries and rounds: in 2017 the wording was changed in Finland, Norway and Sweden but not in Denmark (p. 4)
robustness_checks: re-ran the analysis only for men and women with children under 14 years of age living in the household; results stated not to differ substantially (p. 6)
unresolved_confounders: support for caring fathers is unmeasured: the EVS items cover only the mother's role, and the authors note multiple gender ideologies may coexist (Grunow, Begall, & Buchler, 2018)
other structural and individual factors behind leave take-up, which the authors say make a one-to-one causal relationship between attitudes and take-up unlikely

estimator.value: cross-tabulation of the percentage agreeing by education group, summarised by a gamma coefficient with significance stars

estimation.specification: unconditional bivariate association between education group and binary agreement; the paper prints no estimating equation

heterogeneity.finding: The paper reports that the association between education and this attitude differs across countries and states: "This correlation appears lowest in Denmark and Iceland." (p. 6)
